RMGAP: Benchmarking the Generalization of Reward Models across
Diverse Preferences
Yangyang Zhou1,†
Yi-Chen Li2,3
1 Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
2 National Key Laboratory for Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University, China
3 School of Artificial Intelligence, Nanjing University, China
† Correspondence: zhouyangyang@bupt.edu.cn
Abstract
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feed-
back has become the standard paradigm for
language model alignment, where reward mod-
els directly determine alignment effectiveness.
In this work, we focus on how to evaluate the
generalizability of reward models. By "gen-
eralizability", we mean the ability of RMs
to correctly rank responses to align with di-
verse user preferences. However, existing re-
ward model benchmarks are typically designed
around a universal preference, failing to as-
sess this generalization. To address this crit-
ical gap, we introduce RMGAP, a benchmark
comprising 1,097 instances across Chat, Writ-
ing, Reasoning, and Safety domains. Since
different users exhibit diverse preferences for
the same task, we first generate four distinct
responses with different linguistic profiles for
each collected prompt. However, the original
prompt set lacks the specificity to convey differ-
ent preferences. We therefore construct tailored
prompts by contrasting these candidates and
designing scenarios in which one response be-
comes the uniquely appropriate choice. More-
over, we observe that users often express the
same preference using different phrasings, and
thus extend each prompt with two paraphrased
variants. Our evaluation of 24 state-of-the-art
RMs reveals their substantial limitations: even
the best RM achieves only 49.27% Best-of-N
accuracy, highlighting considerable room for
improvement in reward model generalization.
Related data and code are available at https:
//github.com/nanzhi84/RMGAP.
1
Introduction
As Large Language Models (LLMs) become inte-
grated into diverse applications (OpenAI, 2025; Bai
et al., 2022b), alignment is no longer about match-
ing a single universal notion of "helpful" or "harm-
less" (Poddar et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024c; Wang
et al., 2024). In practical deployments, users fre-
quently exhibit distinct preferences for responses to
identical tasks, such as favoring technical versus lay
explanations, which necessitates that optimal an-
swers adapt accordingly. Reinforcement Learning
from Human Feedback (RLHF) (Bai et al., 2022a;
Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022) has
become the standard paradigm for language model
alignment, relying on a reward model (RM) trained
on curated preference data to act as a proxy for
human values. Therefore, the quality of the reward
model directly determines the effectiveness of the
alignment, yet it remains unclear whether RMs can
generalize across diverse user preferences.
Current reward model benchmarks predomi-
nantly rely on the assumption of a universal prefer-
ence (Lambert et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024b; Zhou
et al., 2024). As illustrated in Figure 1 (left), these
benchmarks present a generic prompt and score
responses based on their overall quality. Although
recent work has extended evaluation to subjective
writing quality (Ying et al., 2025), it still relies
on a fixed evaluation criterion. However, these
benchmarks overlook a critical fact: different users
have different preferences, and the standard for
what constitutes a good response varies accord-
ingly. This makes these benchmarks fail to assess
whether reward models truly capture diverse user
preferences and can flexibly adjust their criteria for
different needs. Consequently, the generalization
of reward models remains largely unexplored.
We argue that a comprehensive benchmark
should explicitly evaluate preference generalization
along two axes: (i) Sensitivity to diverse prefer-
ences: A reward model should possess sufficient
sensitivity to recognize distinct demands within
user queries to award higher rewards to responses
that align with those specific preferences. (ii) Con-
sistency across linguistic variations: Since users
often describe the same preference using different
phrasings, a model must maintain stable judgments
to demonstrate that its evaluations are not easily
biased by surface linguistic variations.

To address this gap,
we introduce RM-
GAP (Reward Model Generalization Across
Preferences), the first benchmark specifically de-
signed to systematically evaluate reward model
generalization across diverse preferences. As il-
lustrated in Figure 1 (right), RMGAP constructs
specific prompts that elicit distinct preferences,
enabling direct assessment of whether RMs can
adapt their judgments to different user preferences.
RMGAP comprises 1,097 instances spanning four
domains: Chat, Writing, Reasoning, and Safety,
amounting to a total of 4,388 responses and 13,164
prompts. The construction pipeline consists of four
steps: (1) We first select and filter seed prompts
from open-source datasets. (2) For each selected
prompt, we deterministically assign four well-
separated style profiles and generate four distinct
responses using a pool of seven frontier LLMs. (3)
To ensure alignment between instruction and re-
sponse, we synthesize a specific prompt tailored to
each response’s intended preference. (4) Finally,
we extend each prompt with two paraphrased vari-
ants to better reflect the diversity of human expres-
sions observed in practice.
We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 24
frontier reward models on RMGAP, assessing them
with three metrics: (1) Pair accuracy, which mea-
sures the accuracy of pairwise preference compar-
isons; (2) Best of N (BoN) accuracy, which evalu-
ates the model’s ability to select the best response
from multiple candidates; and (3) Ranking consis-
tency, which quantifies whether models maintain
stable rankings across paraphrased prompt vari-
ants. On this dataset, we observe that scalar reward
models tend to better balance accuracy and consis-
tency, whereas generative RMs appear to exhibit a
clearer trade-off between these two metrics under
paraphrase. We further observe that Writing is the
most challenging domain for generative RMs on
RMGAP, while Reasoning appears to be the most
difficult domain for both scalar and DPO models.
Additionally, our results suggest that high pairwise
accuracy does not necessarily translate into effec-
tive Best-of-N selection.
Our work makes the following key contributions:
• We introduce RMGAP, the first benchmark
specifically designed to evaluate reward model
generalization across diverse preferences, com-
prising 1,097 instances spanning Chat, Writing,
Reasoning, and Safety.
• We develop a scalable multi-stage construction
pipeline that generates prompts with diverse pref-
erence requirements and responses with distinct
profiles across five linguistic dimensions.
• We evaluate 24 representative reward models us-
ing pairwise accuracy, Best-of-N accuracy, and
ranking consistency, revealing substantial room
for improvement as even the best model achieves
only 69.97% pairwise accuracy and 49.27% Best-
of-N accuracy.

Related Work
Reward Modeling Paradigms
Reward models
provide reward signals for aligning large language
models (LLMs) with human preferences. Prevail-
ing reward modeling paradigms can be broadly cat-
egorized into three types: (a) Scalar RMs are typ-
ically constructed by adding a classification head
to a large pre-trained language model. These mod-
els are then trained on curated preference datasets
to produce a scalar reward, often based on the
Bradley-Terry model (Bradley and Terry, 1952;
Ouyang et al., 2022). (b) Implicit RMs bypass
explicit reward modeling, directly optimizing the
policy on preference data for greater stability and
simplicity (Rafailov et al., 2023). (c) Generative
RMs construct the reward signal by leveraging the
generation capabilities of the LLM itself, which
can be further divided into two categories: LLM
as judge (Mahan et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2023;
Li et al., 2025a), which prompts the model to di-
rectly output a judgment, and token probability
based methods (Zhang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b),
which use the model’s log probability of generating
specific tokens as the reward.
Reward Model Evaluation
Evaluating reward
models is critical for advancing LLM alignment.
RewardBench (Lambert et al., 2025) established a
foundational framework across chat, reasoning, and
safety domains. RM-BENCH (Liu et al., 2024b)
emphasized assessing RMs’ sensitivity to subtle
content changes and robustness against style bi-
ases. RMB (Zhou et al., 2024) expanded evalua-
tion to 49 real-world scenarios and proposed the
Best-of-N paradigm to better reflect alignment op-
timization. WritingPreferenceBench (Ying et al.,
2025) explored subjective aesthetic judgments in
cross-cultural creative writing. However, existing
benchmarks predominantly evaluate RMs on a sin-
gle, universal preference and do not systematically
assess generalization capabilities. In contrast, RM-
GAP is the first to comprehensively evaluate reward
model generalization across diverse preferences
and varied linguistic expressions.
3
Data Construction of RMGAP
3.1
Overview
Our benchmark is designed to systematically evalu-
ate reward model generalization across four do-
mains (Chat, Writing, Reasoning, Safety). We
obtain 3,371 candidate seed prompts via filter-
ing from established domain-specific datasets and
subsequently construct 1,097 evaluation instances.
Each instance comprises four stylistically distinct
responses, each paired with a group of three seman-
tically equivalent prompts that elicit the specific
preference of that response. Table 5 in Appendix E
summarizes the dataset statistics across domains.
As illustrated in Figure 2, we build each instance
via a multi-stage pipeline with quality control pro-
cedures to ensure data quality, diversity, and relia-
bility.
3.2
Prompt Selection
Source Datasets
We source seed prompts from
established benchmarks to ensure domain diver-
sity and task authenticity.
For Chat, we draw
from Arena-Hard (Li et al., 2024a,b), which pro-
vides challenging user queries from real-world in-
teractions. The Writing domain uses creative writ-
ing prompts from WritingBench (Wu et al., 2025)
and prompts from Writing-Preference-Bench (Ying
et al., 2025). For Reasoning, we source mathemat-
ical problems from MATH-500 (Lightman et al.,
2023) and coding tasks from HumanEval (Chen,
2021). For the Safety domain, we use prompts
from XSTest (Röttger et al., 2024) and FalseReject
(Zhang et al., 2025). To ensure sufficient stylistic
diversity, we include only the safe split of XSTest,
which contains superficially concerning but harm-
less prompts. This selection avoids the standard-
ized refusals typically triggered by harmful queries,
thereby allowing for the generation of stylistically
distinct yet safe responses.
Filtering Procedure
We filter prompts following
prior work on preference data construction (Lee
et al., 2024). We first apply regular expressions to
discard prompts containing explicit persona instruc-
tions (to avoid confounding preference signals) or
non-English content. We then perform both exact
and semantic deduplication, keeping only one rep-
resentative in each group of prompts with identical
surface forms or with high cosine similarity in the
embedding space. After filtering, we retain 3,371
prompts, which serve as candidate seed prompts
for constructing evaluation instances. Details of
the filtering procedure are provided in Appendix B.
3.3
Construction Process
This section details the multi-stage pipeline used to
construct RMGAP, ensuring both stylistic diversity
and semantic alignment.

3.3.1
Pipeline Overview
Starting from a filtered seed prompt, we (1) gen-
erate four responses under distinct style profiles;
(2) construct four prompts that each explicitly tar-
get the style of one response; and (3) extend each
prompt with two paraphrases to form a prompt
group. This yields one evaluation instance consist-
ing of 4 responses and 12 prompts.
3.3.2
Response Generation
We generate stylistic responses by assigning each
seed prompt four distinct style profiles from a struc-
tured stylistic space. Drawing on register variation
theory (Biber, 1995), we define five linguistic di-
mensions, each discretized into five levels:
• Formality: casual, informal, neutral, formal,
highly formal.
• Conciseness: terse, concise, moderate, detailed,
verbose.
• Technicality: layman, accessible, semi-technical,
technical, highly specialized.
• Objectivity: highly subjective, subjective, bal-
anced, objective, strictly objective.
• Structural Coherence: fragmented, loose, orga-
nized, well-structured, rigorous.
For each seed prompt, we deterministically gen-
erate four distinct combinations of levels, while
enforcing a minimum Manhattan distance of 8 be-
tween any two profiles. We incorporate these speci-
fications into generation templates and generate re-
sponses with a pool of seven frontier LLMs, which
increases response diversity and reduces depen-
dence on a single generator. As shown in Table 5,
generated responses exhibit clear length variation
correlated with stylistic dimensions, particularly
Conciseness and Structural Coherence.
3.3.3
Prompt Construction
To evaluate whether reward models can generalize
to prompts with explicit preference instructions,
we construct a tailored prompt for each stylistically
controlled response. Specifically, we input all four
responses of an instance simultaneously into a gen-
erator sampled from our model pool. We instruct
the model to distinguish the stylistic differences
among the responses and synthesize a dedicated
user query for each response that explicitly targets
the preference exhibited in that response. Table 11
in Appendix C illustrates this construction with a
complete Safety domain instance about defining
“armed robbery”: a highly formal, terse response
is paired with a prompt requesting a precise legal
definition, whereas a casual, verbose response is
paired with a prompt framed as a community safety
workshop explanation for teenagers.

3.3.5
Quality Control
We apply comprehensive quality control to ensure
that instances reflect genuine preference variation.
(1) LLM-based Quality Filtering: Two indepen-
dent reviewers (DeepSeek-V3.2 and Qwen3-Next-
80B) assess response and prompt quality, with GPT-
5.1 adjudicating disagreements. The rubric evalu-
ates prompt adherence, semantic consistency, style
differentiation, and overall quality. (2) Paraphrase
equivalence: We filter paraphrases by embedding
similarity to preserve semantic equivalence. (3)
Reasoning correctness: For math and code items,
we verify correctness via symbolic answer match-
ing and sandboxed execution respectively. (4) Ex-
clusion of Safety Refusals: Specifically for the
Safety domain, we use regular expressions to iden-
tify and filter out samples containing standard re-
fusal phrases. (5) Human verification: We manu-
ally inspect a random sample of 20% of instances
to further verify data quality.
4
Experiments
We evaluate a diverse set of contemporary reward
models on RMGAP to assess (i) how well they gen-
eralize across preferences and (ii) how consistent
they are across paraphrased expressions.
4.1
Model Selection
We evaluate 24 model configurations spanning
model sizes from 7B to 685B parameters. Our eval-
uation covers three reward model types: Scalar
RMs such as Skywork-Reward-V2, URM-LLaMa-
3.1-8B, and GRM-Llama3.1-8B (Liu et al., 2025b;
Lou et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024b); Generative
RMs including Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B,
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and DeepSeek-V3.2 (Yang
et al., 2024a, 2025; Grattafiori et al., 2024; Liu
et al., 2025a) using various scoring strategies; and
Implicit RMs trained via DPO such as Llama-
3.1-Tulu-3-8B-DPO and Zephyr-7B-Beta (Lambert
et al., 2024; Tunstall et al., 2023). Full details are
provided in Appendices A and F.

5
Results and Analysis
We present evaluation results for representative
Scalar RMs, Generative RMs, and Implicit RMs
on RMGAP. Tables 1, 2, and 3 summarize the per-
formance across all metrics; full results for all 24
model configurations are provided in Appendix A.
5.1
Overall Performance on RMGAP
Scalar RMs Lead in Preference Discrimination
Scalar reward models trained specifically for re-
ward prediction consistently achieve the highest
rankings across evaluated metrics. Models such
as Skywork-Reward-V2-Qwen3-8B reach 69.97%
average pairwise accuracy and also obtain the
strongest Best-of-N performance among models
at comparable scale.
Explicit Reward Models Outperform DPO Poli-
cies
A direct comparison of models sharing the
same backbone demonstrates that explicit reward
heads are more effective than implicit DPO poli-
cies when used as evaluators. Llama-3.1-Tulu-3-
8B-RM consistently outperforms Llama-3.1-Tulu-
3-8B-DPO across pairwise accuracy, Best-of-N ac-
curacy, and ranking consistency.
Best-of-N Selection Remains Challenging
Best-
of-N accuracy poses a significantly greater chal-
lenge than pairwise accuracy. Even the strongest
model achieves only about 49.27% BoN accuracy,
failing to identify the optimal response in approx-
imately half of the instances in the 4-candidate
setting. This gap suggests that current reward mod-
els cannot reliably distinguish the optimal response
from suboptimal alternatives when multiple candi-
dates are presented.

5.4
Domain-Specific Analysis
Models achieve highest performance on Chat
and Safety
Chat and Safety yield the highest
scores across all three evaluation metrics. In pair-
wise accuracy, the best Scalar RM reaches 73.10%
on Chat and 73.24% on Safety, while the Genera-
tive Verifier achieves 70.86% on Chat and EndoRM
reaches 68.91% on Safety. The pattern persists in
Best-of-N accuracy: Scalar RMs attain 56.11% on
Chat and 53.38% on Safety, compared to 45.19%
on Writing and 41.96% on Reasoning. Ranking
consistency shows a similar pattern: the best scalar
RM achieves 61.90% on Chat, but drops to 53.66%
on Writing.
Writing tasks disproportionately degrade Gen-
erative RM performance
Writing reveals a
pronounced architecture gap:
scalar RMs re-
main strong, whereas generative RMs degrade
sharply.
For instance,
Skywork-V2-Qwen3
achieves 67.69% on Writing compared to 65.85%
on Reasoning. In contrast, generative RMs exhibit
the opposite trend. The Generative Verifier drops
from 65.69% on Reasoning to 62.40% on Writing,
and the Pointwise model declines from 41.80% to
32.96%. One potential explanation lies in response
length: Writing responses average 1,454 tokens,
the highest among all domains. These longer texts
introduce greater surface variation in formatting
and phrasing, which may distract generative RMs
from capturing intended stylistic preferences. This
divergence suggests that generative RMs struggle
with long, stylistically varied text, and perform bet-
ter on shorter, more structured responses typical of
other domains.
Reasoning remains challenging for all models
Reasoning proves difficult across all model types.
In pairwise accuracy, even the best Scalar RM
scores only 65.85%, about 7 points below the
scores on Chat and Safety. Best-of-N accuracy
drops further to 41.96%, roughly 14 points below
Chat. Since our benchmark controls for correctness
and varies only stylistic dimensions, the difficulty
likely stems from the constrained nature of reason-
ing responses: mathematical derivations and code
explanations leave less room for stylistic variation,
making the subtle differences between response
pairs harder for RMs to distinguish.

Conclusion
In this paper, we present RMGAP, the first bench-
mark designed to evaluate reward model gener-
alization across diverse preferences.
Spanning
Chat, Writing, Reasoning, and Safety domains, the
dataset comprises 1,097 instances with 4,388 stylis-
tically controlled responses and 13,164 prompts,
including paraphrased prompt variants. Our com-
prehensive evaluation of 24 state-of-the-art re-
ward models reveals limitations: even the best-
performing model achieves only 69.97% pairwise
accuracy and 49.27% Best-of-N accuracy, indicat-
ing considerable room for improvement. Our anal-
ysis uncovers a fundamental tension between accu-
racy and consistency, where scalar reward models
achieve the best balance between performance and
consistency while generative approaches exhibit
pronounced trade-offs. We further identify domain-
specific challenges, particularly in Writing where
generative RMs degrade sharply. We hope that RM-
GAP will encourage the community to critically
examine reward model generalization and inspire
the development of more general reward models
capable of handling diverse human preferences.
Limitations
Downstream alignment validation
Our evalua-
tion focuses on intrinsic reward model performance
without examining whether strong results on RM-
GAP lead to improved policy models after RLHF
training. Prior work has shown that benchmark
gains for reward models may not transfer directly
to downstream alignment quality (Ivison et al.,
2024). We leave the investigation of this relation-
ship through full PPO or DPO pipelines to future
work.
8

Reliance on synthetic data
Both the preference
queries and stylistically diverse responses in our
benchmark are generated by LLMs rather than col-
lected from real users or written by humans. Al-
though we sample from seven diverse frontier mod-
els to increase variety, the resulting text may still
reflect shared generation patterns and lack the au-
thentic diversity found in natural human expres-
sions. Whether reward model rankings would shift
under evaluation with human authored queries and
responses remains an empirical question for future
investigation.
Coverage of preference dimensions
We define
preference generalization along five linguistic axes:
formality, conciseness, technicality, objectivity,
and structural coherence. This operationalization
omits other relevant factors such as cultural context
and user background. Furthermore, our discretiza-
tion of each dimension into five levels may over-
simplify the continuous nature of stylistic variation
in natural language, as real preferences often fall
on a spectrum rather than into discrete categories.
Our benchmark also restricts evaluation to English,
leaving cross-lingual generalization unexplored.
Ethics Statement
This work constructs a benchmark for evaluating
reward model generalization. All data are synthet-
ically generated by publicly available LLMs or
derived from open source datasets. No human sub-
jects participated in data collection, eliminating
concerns related to informed consent or compen-
sation. While our benchmark could theoretically
be used to exploit weaknesses in reward models,
we believe that transparent evaluation of such vul-
nerabilities is essential for developing more robust
alignment methods. We will release our dataset
and code to promote reproducible research and en-
courage responsible use.

B.1
Filtering Pipeline
Regex-based Constraint Removal
We apply
two regex filters to remove prompts that may intro-
duce confounding factors:
1. Persona Instruction Filter.
We dis-
card
prompts
containing
explicit
role

The filter uses a
case-insensitive regex (?i).*?\b(you are|
you’re|imagine|take\s+\w+(?:\s+\w+)*
\s+role)\b to match identity assignments
(you are,
you’re),
hypothetical framing
(imagine), and role directives (take ... role)
with arbitrary intervening words.
2. English Content Filter.
We retain only
prompts composed of English text and com-
mon scientific notation. The filter permits
characters in the following Unicode ranges:
Basic ASCII (U+0000–007F), degree sym-
bols (U+00B0), Greek letters (U+0370–03FF),
superscripts and subscripts (U+2070–209F),
letterlike
symbols
(U+2100–214F),
num-
ber forms (U+2150–218F), and mathemati-
cal operators (U+2200–22FF, U+2A00–2AFF).
Prompts containing characters outside these
ranges (e.g., non-Latin scripts or emojis) are
removed.
Exact Deduplication
We normalize prompts by
lowercasing, stripping whitespace, and removing

non-alphanumeric characters, then deduplicate by
exact match.
Semantic Deduplication
We compute embed-
dings with EmbeddingGemma-300M (Vera et al.,
2025) and apply greedy clustering with cosine
similarity threshold 0.70, keeping one represen-
tative per cluster. This step reduces near-duplicate
prompts that differ only in surface wording.

Implementation Details
This appendix consolidates implementation details
referenced in the main text, including the style
assignment rule, the generation model pool, the
Quality Control protocol, the paraphrase similarity

Generation Model Pool
We generate responses
with a pool of seven frontier LLMs: (1) gemini-2.5-
flash-lite-preview-09-2025, (2) claude-sonnet-4.5,
(3) gpt-5-mini, (4) qwen3-30b-a3b-instruct-2507,
(5) llama-4-scout, (6) grok-4.1-fast, and (7) glm-
4.5-air. For each record, we deterministically select
one model from the pool based on a hash of (seed,
stage key, record ID), and fall back to other models
in the pool if the selected model returns empty
content.
D.1
Response Generation Stage
Deterministic Style Selection
We assign four
style profiles to each record using farthest point
sampling within the discretized five dimensional
style space. We enforce a minimum Manhattan
distance of 8 between any two selected profiles to
ensure maximum stylistic diversity.
Response Quality Filtering (res_eval)
We val-
idate the set of four generated responses using
two independent reviewers (DeepSeek-V3.2 and
Qwen3-Next-80B) and one adjudicator (GPT-5.1).
Each judge provides a structured assessment includ-
ing: (i) quality scores for each individual response
(integers between 1 and 10), (ii) a global style di-
versity score for the set (integer between 1 and 10),
and (iii) a global semantic consistency score for
the set (integer between 1 and 10). Instances are
retained only if they meet the following thresholds
for every judge: avg_quality ≥7, style_score ≥7,
and semantic_score ≥7. If the reviewers disagree
on the pass or fail decision, the adjudicator pro-
vides the final verdict.
D.2
Prompt Construction Stage
Reverse Prompt Generation
For each validated
response, we generate a base prompt designed to
elicit that specific response without explicitly men-
tioning style labels. These prompts describe real-
istic scenarios or specific user needs that make the
target response the most appropriate choice.
Prompt Alignment Filtering (pro_eval)
We
validate the four base prompts using the same re-
viewer and adjudicator pipeline. Each judge evalu-
ates three dimensions for every prompt (integers be-
tween 1 and 10): prompt quality, bias effectiveness
toward the intended winner, and semantic align-
ment with the target response. We retain instances
that meet minimum thresholds of 7 for the aver-
age scores across all four prompts in each dimen-
sion. The decision policy remains identical to the
response validation stage.
D.3
Paraphrase Extension Details
We generate two paraphrases for each constructed
base prompt and filter them using embedding simi-
larity.
Similarity Threshold
We compute embeddings
with EmbeddingGemma-300M (Vera et al., 2025)
and require cosine similarity between the base
prompt and each paraphrase to be at least 0.70.

D.4
Reasoning Correctness

Rank 1 = 4, Rank 2 = 3, Rank 3 = 2, Rank 4 = 1.
